SECTION 010:00–2:36

Check consistency before finding the solutions

A relation among the left-hand sides must also hold on the right.

Lecture 8 solves the full problem Ax = b: first determine whether a solution exists, then find one solution or the entire family. It uses the same three-by-four matrix as Lecture 7:

A=[1222246836810]

Row 3 equals row 1 plus row 2. For a solution x, the same relation must hold among the corresponding right-hand sides:

b₃ = b₁ + b₂.

If b₁ = 1 and b₂ = 5, the only possible third entry is b₃ = 6. Choosing b₃ = 17 instead makes the equations inconsistent.

This reasoning is independent of any attempt to calculate x. A combination of left-hand sides that is identically zero must be matched by the same zero combination on the right.

The first question

Before finding all solutions, check whether the right-hand side obeys every row-dependence condition.

SECTION 022:36–5:45

Carry the right-hand side through elimination

Apply every row operation to the augmented matrix [A | b].

Append b as an extra column to form [A | b]. The vertical divider distinguishes the coefficient columns from the right-hand side, but a row operation must act on the entire row.

Clear the first column with R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁ and R₃ ← R₃ − 3R₁. The new lower coefficient rows are both (0, 0, 2, 4), while their right-hand sides are b₂ − 2b₁ and b₃ − 3b₁.

Subtract the new row 2 from the new row 3. The coefficient row becomes zero, and its right-hand side is

(b₃ − 3b₁) − (b₂ − 2b₁) = b₃ − b₂ − b₁.

The final augmented system therefore represents

x₁ + 2x₂ + 2x₃ + 2x₄ = b₁,
2x₃ + 4x₄ = b₂ − 2b₁,
0 = b₃ − b₂ − b₁.

The last equation is a consistency test. It confirms the row-relation condition from the opening section. In this example, satisfying it is also sufficient: the other two rows have pivots, so they can be solved after choosing the free variables.

SECTION 035:45–10:12

Recognize the same consistency condition in two ways

Column combinations and row dependencies give equivalent tests.

Take the consistent choice b = (1, 5, 6)ᵀ. The transformed right-hand side is (1, 3, 0)ᵀ, giving

x₁ + 2x₂ + 2x₃ + 2x₄ = 1,
2x₃ + 4x₄ = 3,
0 = 0.

There are two equivalent descriptions of when Ax = b is solvable. The first is the column-space statement from earlier lectures:

Ax = b is solvable ⇔ b ∈ C(A).

The second uses dependencies among the rows. Whenever a linear combination of A’s rows gives the zero row, the same combination of the entries of b must give zero.

All such row relations are required. Checking only one arbitrarily chosen relation need not be sufficient for a different matrix. Elimination checks the independent conditions by looking at every zero coefficient row it creates.

Compact notation. If yᵀA = 0, consistency requires yᵀb = 0. This notation expresses the lecture’s row-combination statement. For this A, yᵀ = (−1, −1, 1) gives −b₁ − b₂ + b₃ = 0.

SECTION 0410:12–15:42

Set free variables to zero to find a particular solution

Solve only for the pivot variables once consistency is established.

To find one convenient solution, set every free variable to zero. For this matrix the pivot columns are 1 and 3, while columns 2 and 4 are free.

Choose x₂ = 0 and x₄ = 0.

The two nonzero echelon equations reduce to

x₁ + 2x₃ = 1,
2x₃ = 3.

Back substitution gives x₃ = 3/2, then x₁ = 1 − 2(3/2) = −2. Thus a particular solution is

xp=[−203/20]

Check it in the original system:

[1222246836810][−203/20]=[156]

Setting the free variables to zero is a convenient convention for selecting one member of the solution family. Other choices can give other particular solutions. For the fixed zero-free-variable choice, the pivot variables are uniquely determined.

SECTION 0515:42–17:50

Add the nullspace to obtain every solution

All solutions differ from a particular solution by a nullspace vector.

Let xₚ be one solution of Ax = b. Any nullspace vector xₙ satisfies Axₙ = 0. Therefore

A(xₚ + xₙ) = Axₚ + Axₙ = b + 0 = b.

Adding a nullspace vector preserves the right-hand side. This produces a family of solutions.

It also produces every possible solution. If x is any solution, subtract the particular one:

A(x − xₚ) = Ax − Axₚ = b − b = 0.

So x − xₚ belongs to N(A), and x can be written as xₚ plus a nullspace vector. Hence the complete solution is

x = xₚ + xₙ,   xₙ ∈ N(A).
Converse made explicit. The lecture explains why adding nullspace vectors works and states the complete solution. The subtraction argument here verifies that no solutions are omitted.

SECTION 0617:50–21:09

Write the complete two-parameter solution

Use the two special solutions from Lecture 7.

For the same matrix, Lecture 7 found two independent special solutions of Ax = 0:

s1=[−2100],s2=[20−21]

Combining them with xₚ gives

x = xₚ + cs₁ + ds₂,   c, d ∈ R.
x=[−203/20]+c[−2100]+d[20−21]

In coordinates, this is

x = (−2 − 2c + 2d, c, 3/2 − 2d, d)ᵀ.

The free coordinates are x₂ = c and x₄ = d. Every pair of real values gives a solution, and every solution is represented by exactly one such pair.

Keep the particular part fixed

The coefficients c and d are arbitrary. The coefficient of xₚ is fixed at 1: scaling it would scale b too.

SECTION 0721:09–24:30

The solution set is a shifted nullspace

For nonzero b, the solution family does not pass through zero.

Every input x has four components, so these solution vectors live in R⁴. The two independent nullspace directions span a two-dimensional subspace of that ambient space.

Adding the fixed vector xₚ translates the entire nullspace. Its shape and directions are unchanged, but it now passes through xₚ instead of the origin.

Solution set = xₚ + N(A).

This is an affine plane: a translated two-dimensional subspace. It is not a subspace for this nonzero b, because A0 = 0 is not b, so the origin is missing.

The word “plane” describes the two parameters, not the number of components of its vectors. The schematic figure represents the relationship between two parallel sets; their actual vectors remain four-component vectors.

The procedure is now complete: check consistency, find a particular solution, compute the nullspace, and add every nullspace vector to that particular solution.

SECTION 0824:30–26:44

Use the rank to organize the possibilities

An m × n matrix can have at most min(m, n) pivots.

For the general discussion, let A have m rows, n columns, and rank r. A pivot uses one row and one column, and neither can contain two pivots. Therefore

r ≤ m,   r ≤ n,
so r ≤ min(m, n).

Rank is the number of independent pivot equations and pivot variables. There are n − r free variables. Elimination leaves m − r zero coefficient rows, each of which must have zero on the transformed right-hand side for consistency.

The largest possible rank for a matrix of that shape is min(m, n). Full column rank means every column gets a pivot, r = n. Full row rank means every row gets a pivot, r = m. Both are possible at once only for a square matrix with full rank.

Existence and uniqueness answer different questions

Having a pivot in every row guarantees a solution for every b. Having a pivot in every column guarantees at most one solution for any b.

The remaining sections examine these possibilities through concrete examples and summarize them in four cases.

SECTION 0926:44–30:13

Full column rank gives uniqueness whenever a solution exists

No free variables means the nullspace is {0}.

If r = n, there is a pivot in every column. Thus n − r = 0: there are no free variables and no nonzero special solutions.

Full column rank: r = n.
N(A) = {0}.

For a consistent right-hand side, the complete solution x = xₚ + xₙ reduces to x = xₚ, because xₙ can only be zero. So there is exactly one solution if there is one at all.

The absence of free variables does not by itself guarantee existence. When m > n, the extra rows can impose consistency conditions on b. Such a matrix has either zero or one solution for a given b.

The reduced form is an identity over zero rows:

R = [ Iₙ ; 0 ].

For a square matrix, the zero-row block is absent. The next example is strictly tall, with more equations than unknowns, so both the inconsistent and unique-solution possibilities occur.

SECTION 1030:13–34:55

A tall matrix can have zero or one solution

The two columns are independent, but they do not fill R⁴.

Strang’s full-column-rank example is

T=[13216151]

The two columns are not multiples, so rank(T) = 2, equal to the number of columns. The reduced form is

RT=[10010000]

The column space is two-dimensional inside R⁴. Some four-component b lie outside it and have no solution. For instance, b = (1, 0, 0, 0)ᵀ is impossible: rows 2 and 3 would force 2x₁ + x₂ = 0 and 6x₁ + x₂ = 0, hence x₁ = x₂ = 0, contradicting row 1.

For a consistent example, add the two columns:

[13216151][11]=[4376]

The input (1, 1)ᵀ is the only solution for that right-hand side. There is no nullspace freedom to add.

Labels and extra check. The lecture reuses A for its examples. Here T labels the tall matrix. The explicit inconsistent right-hand side is an editorial illustration of the lecture’s zero-or-one conclusion.

SECTION 1134:55–39:51

Full row rank guarantees existence for every right-hand side

With more columns than rows, free variables leave infinitely many solutions.

If r = m, every row has a pivot. There are no zero coefficient rows to impose a consistency condition on the transformed right-hand side. Thus Ax = b has a solution for every b in Rᵐ.

There are n − r = n − m free variables. If n > m, this number is positive, so every right-hand side has infinitely many solutions.

The lecture obtains its example by transposing the tall matrix:

W=[12653111]

The first two columns are independent, so columns 1 and 2 become the pivot identity. Completing the numerical row reduction gives

RW=[10−4/5−3/50117/514/5]

There are two pivot variables and two free variables. Any right-hand side is attainable; the two free values parameterize the whole solution family.

SECTION 1239:51–42:33

Full rank in a square matrix gives exactly one solution for every b

Both existence and uniqueness hold when r = m = n.

When r = m = n, the matrix is square and every row and column has a pivot. It is invertible, and its reduced form is the identity.

Full row rank guarantees a solution for every two-component b. Full column rank guarantees uniqueness. Together they give exactly one solution for each right-hand side.

SECTION 1342:33–47:08

Summarize the four rank cases

Rank controls consistency and the number of free parameters.

The lecture finishes by organizing the solution counts. Over the real numbers, a consistent linear system has either exactly one solution or infinitely many; each free variable can vary through all real values.

Rank conditionRight-hand sidesNumber of solutions for a fixed b
r = m = nEvery bExactly one
r = n < mOnly b in C(A)Zero or one
r = m < nEvery bInfinitely many
r < m and r < nOnly b in C(A)Zero or infinitely many

The existence question is governed by the rows: r = m means there are no zero coefficient rows imposing restrictions on b. If r < m, some right-hand sides are inconsistent.

The uniqueness question is governed by the columns: r = n means there are no free variables. If r < n, any consistent system has n − r free parameters and therefore infinitely many solutions.

The complete picture

Check that b is attainable. Then find xₚ and add N(A). Rank tells you how many free parameters remain.
